mcqs.question: An instance has averaged 8% CPU utilization for a month. What does rightsizing recommend, and why is it safe?
options: Downsize to an instance with headroom above the actual usage pattern, since the unused capacity wasn't reserved for a real spike
Leave it as-is, because changing instance size always risks an outage
Upsize it, since low CPU utilization usually means the instance is underpowered
Switch it to spot pricing only, without changing the instance size
mcqs.explanation: Sustained low utilization over weeks means the extra capacity is genuinely unused, not reserved headroom for a real peak — downsizing to a size with real headroom is safe and proportionally cheaper. Low CPU is the opposite signal from underpowered; changing size doesn't inherently risk an outage if headroom is preserved.

mcqs.question: Which of these is the best example of an orphaned resource costing money with zero benefit to any workload?
options: A load balancer actively routing traffic to three healthy application instances
An unattached disk left behind after the VM that used it was deleted
A reserved instance covering a team's steady production baseline
A compute-optimized instance running a CPU-bound nightly batch job
mcqs.explanation: An unattached disk serves nothing once its VM is gone — pure orphaned cost. The other options are all actively serving a real workload or commitment, so they aren't waste even though they cost money.

mcqs.question: A workload is bottlenecked on disk throughput, not CPU or memory. Which family choice fixes this?
options: A compute-optimized family with more vCPUs
A memory-optimized family with more RAM
A family with high network/disk throughput matched to the actual I/O bottleneck
Any family works equally, since instance family only affects CPU speed
mcqs.explanation: Matching family to the actual bottleneck is the point — an I/O-bound workload gets no benefit from more vCPUs or RAM if the disk path is what's saturated. Instance families differ meaningfully in network/disk throughput, not just CPU.

mcqs.question: Why is 'rightsize once and move on' a flawed strategy?
options: Rightsizing tools only produce accurate recommendations the first time they're run
Usage patterns drift over time, so a fleet sized correctly today can become mis-sized again within months
Cloud providers charge an extra fee each time you rightsize a resource
Instance prices change only once per year, so re-checking sizing is unnecessary
mcqs.explanation: Traffic and usage patterns are not static, so a correct sizing decision decays over time in either direction. None of the other options describe a real constraint on rightsizing.
